title: Epilogue. The Science Behind the Children

blocks.text: This book is a novel, a sequel to *The Daughter of Two Worlds* and *Letters from the Stars*. Aya, Andrés, Lía, the clone, Nexum, the ship's seedbed and the civilisations sown here on other worlds are fiction. What follows is not. Here we separate, as carefully as we can, what already existed in 2026 (with date and source) from what still belongs to the realm of speculation or dream. Nothing written in these pages replaces the judgement of a healthcare professional.

blocks.text: **There are robots with a human form, and they are not people.** On 20 November 2000, Honda presented ASIMO in Tokyo: a 120-centimetre bipedal robot able to walk, climb stairs and recognise people and gestures, according to the company's official press release (https://global.honda/en/newsroom/news/2000/c001120b-eng.html). Since then, other laboratories and companies have shown humanoid-looking machines, each more agile than the last. That is engineering: metal, sensors, software. It is not a cultivated body, with skin, blood and a chip behind the nape, able to wait on a doorstep and to want to stay. Aya, in this saga, remains a dream of the novel, not a product in a catalogue.

blocks.text: **Models that imitate very early stages of a human embryo can be built in the laboratory; they are not embryos, and they cannot be implanted.** On 27 June 2023, *Nature* published “Pluripotent stem cell-derived model of the post-implantation human embryo” by Bailey A. T. Weatherbee, Magdalena Zernicka-Goetz and their team at the University of Cambridge and collaborators (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06368-y). The work describes a three-dimensional structure obtained from pluripotent stem cells that reproduces some processes of the second week of development, a stage that is normally hidden because the embryo implants in the uterus.

blocks.text: On 6 September 2023, *Nature* published “Complete human day 14 post-implantation embryo models from naive ES cells”, led by Jacob H. Hanna at the Weizmann Institute of Science (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06604-5). Starting from human embryonic stem cells that had not been genetically modified, the team obtained integrated models that recapitulated the organisation of almost all the lineages and compartments of a human embryo about fourteen days after fertilisation, without using an egg, sperm or a uterus. The authors themselves stressed that they were far from being able to create an embryo from scratch, and that this was a model for studying a window of development that had until then been very difficult to observe.

blocks.text: **International guidelines prohibit transferring these models to a uterus, and also human reproductive cloning.** On 27 May 2021, *Stem Cell Reports* published “ISSCR Guidelines for Stem Cell Research and Clinical Translation: The 2021 update” by Robin Lovell-Badge and the working group of the International Society for Stem Cell Research (https://www.cell.com/stem-cell-reports/fulltext/S2213-6711(21)00263-0). These guidelines are not law, but they are the most widely cited ethical reference in the field: among other things, they classify as not permitted the transfer of a stem-cell-derived embryo model to the uterus of a human being or an animal, and human reproductive cloning. The ISSCR has also warned against the expression “synthetic embryo”, because it is inaccurate and causes confusion: these models are not embryos and, according to the society, do not and will not have the potential to develop into the equivalent of a born human being (https://www.isscr.org/isscr-news/isscr-statement-on-new-research-with-embryo-models).

blocks.text: **A mammal has been cloned from an adult cell; people are not cloned.** Dolly the sheep was born on 5 July 1996. On 27 February 1997, *Nature* published the work of Ian Wilmut and colleagues, “Viable offspring derived from fetal and adult mammalian cells” (https://www.nature.com/articles/385810a0). In Spain, Law 14/2006 of 26 May on assisted human reproduction techniques expressly prohibits “the cloning of human beings for reproductive purposes” (Article 1.3) (https://www.boe.es/buscar/act.php?id=BOE-A-2006-9292). (The quotation from the Spanish law is our own translation.) A ship's seedbed that manufactures peoples of humanoids in the image of the earthly man is a premise of this novel, not an existing or authorised procedure.

blocks.text: **The idea of deliberately seeding life on another world has been put forward as a hypothesis, not as a fact.** In July 1973, the journal *Icarus* published “Directed panspermia” by Francis H. C. Crick and Leslie E. Orgel (https://doi.org/10.1016/0019-1035(73)90110-3). The authors considered the possibility that life had reached the Earth sent deliberately by a civilisation on another planet, and concluded that this was possible, but that the scientific evidence was, at the time, insufficient to say anything about its likelihood. It was informed speculation, not a demonstration. It neither authorises nor describes the act of founding humanoid civilisations in other star systems.

blocks.text: **Nobody has created a humanoid with a cultivated body and a chip-mind, and nobody has sown a people on another planet.** In 2026 there are no cultivated human wombs, nor any civilisation of “children of the Earth” under two suns, in an eternal twilight or in a valley that copies Lo Pagán. There is no workshop aboard a ship capable of placing the memory of a lagoon in a chip. There is no crewed journey to another star system, as the epilogue of *Letters from the Stars* already said. The embryo models of 2023 are kept in the laboratory for a short time, for research purposes; they do not walk, do not ask questions, do not dig a cistern or build a ship to go home.

blocks.text: This novel imagines that, decades after 2060, some of these impossibilities are crossed, because the laws and techniques of one age do not always coincide with those of the next. That is a premise of fiction, not a prediction.

blocks.text: The clone sows peoples and then says they are no longer his. Andrés receives those sowings without having set foot in them. Aya, who was made for a house, hears of peoples made for a planet. Lía, who chose winter, has brothers and sisters from a sky who may or may not grow old, and who may one day ask to come in to this shore. That question (what a child of the Earth is if they have never set foot on the Earth, who has the right to sow a world, whether the one who sows is a father or an author, whether a door should open to someone who comes from a portrait) is ethical, not technical, and no scientific paper will settle it. The science of 2026 can already make a machine with a human form walk, model on a dish the first days of a development, and forbid, at least on paper, that such a model be taken to a uterus. It cannot yet tell us what we should do if one day the universe truly came to look like a family.
